stories.headline: Kyrie Irving returns to Mavs, dazzles in China preseason game
stories.summary: Kyrie Irving dazzled in his return to the Mavericks, scoring 17 points in his first game in 586 days.
stories.body:
MACAO, China -- The Dallas Mavericks called a play for Kyrie Irving on the opening possession of his first game in 586 days, much to the delight of the Venetian Arena sellout crowd that roared when the eight-time All-Star caught the ball on the right wing.

Irving delivered, driving by Jabari Smith Jr. for a reverse layup, setting off a celebration on the Dallas bench and eliciting an even louder roar from the Chinese fans who enthusiastically welcomed him back after he missed all of last season while recovering from a torn ACL in his left knee.

"A lot of emotions leading into it," Irving said. "Grateful that Dusty [May] called the first play for me. Had my mind made up just to attack. ... I saw that baseline open up a little bit, and it just felt good to get that out of the way.

"I was imagining how it was going to go, dreaming about how it was going to go. I'm just glad I got that out of the way."

Irving finished with 17 points on 6-of-13 shooting in 22 minutes during the Mavericks' 132-115 preseason win over the Houston Rockets on Sunday night.

"I didn't expect him to play this well after being off for so long, just [because of] the rhythm of the game," May said. "It's just a testament to his work."

It was Irving's first game action since he tore the ACL in his left knee on March 3, 2025. He revealed this week that he sustained a Grade 2 calf strain in December, interrupting his rehabilitation and factoring into the decision to rule him out for the season after the All-Star break.

"He's back to being who he is," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said. "He'll only get better as he gets his rhythm back in real NBA games."

Irving sat out the preseason opener Friday as part of the Mavericks' plan to ease him back into action. He led the Mavericks in scoring in his return and dished out the ball for three assists.

"Being able to perform at a high level, that felt amazing," Irving said. "I humbled myself while also just being aggressive and trying to look like myself again."

It was the 34-year-old Irving's first time playing alongside reigning Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg.

One highlight of the Dallas star duo's first outing together was Flagg throwing a full-court pass to Irving for a transition layup early in the second quarter. Early in the third, Flagg had a spectacular chase-down block on Houston's Amen Thompson, igniting a fast break that Irving finished with a pull-up 3-pointer.

"That was really cool to see, to be able to witness that," Mavericks guard Max Christie said of Irving's performance. "He looked phenomenal. It was very, very fun to watch."

stories.headline: Andy Burnham to publish Man City mayoral dealings after intervention draws criticism
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the club's owners raised eyebrows.
stories.body:
Andy Burnham has said he will publish all details of his dealings with Manchester City in his previous mayoral role after his intervention in support of the club's owners raised eyebrows.

Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch had urged him to publish "everything" related to his work with the club as Greater Manchester mayor.

City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club maintain their innocence and have appealed against the verdict.

Burnham said last month he would be "really concerned" if City's Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the finding, crediting them with being "a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester."

Downing Street sought to clarify his comments afterwards, saying the Prime Minister was clear the judgment is serious and that where wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the consequences.

Burnham said he would "put out there" everything he had done to work with the club's owners as mayor in an interview with the Rest is Politics podcast to be released on Monday.

He said that "the football issues are different from the investment issues."

He added: "But I see now people trying to conflate these things. I've been asked by the Leader of the Opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do.

"I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester.

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021. That is right and I will put that all out there.

"But the football issues, they are serious and have to be dealt with, and the process is independent and it has to run its course. But I think everybody should separate the investment issues because they're not the same thing."

The Premier League said an independent commission found City arranged "sham" commercial deals with a number of their sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were required to pay only a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.

The commission found that the remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan's Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd, which majority-owned the club.

Shadow sports minister Louie French called for Burnham to also "come clean" about any meetings since becoming Prime Minister and urged Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy to respond to questions.

He said: "The Prime Minister must publish every contact between his ministers, officials and Manchester City since he walked into Number 10, the Prime Minister must also explain why he inappropriately intervened in this case, and Lisa Nandy must answer the questions I have put to her in full."

stories.headline: Dodgers keep Miguel Rojas on NLCS roster; Brewers hold steady
stories.summary: Miguel Rojas is on the NLCS roster for the Dodgers after being sidelined by lower back pain, while the Brewers made no changes from the NLDS.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Miguel Rojas is on the National League Championship Series roster for the Los Angeles Dodgers after being sidelined by lower back pain.

Left-hander Justin Wrobleski also is part of the Dodgers' roster for their matchup with the Milwaukee Brewers, who went with the same 26-man group that they had for their NL Division Series against the San Diego Padres.

Game 1 of the NLCS is on Sunday night.

Rojas underwent testing after he left the Dodgers' 3-1 victory at the Atlanta Braves in Game 3 of their NLDS. The imaging mostly showed prior back issues.

The veteran infielder worked out with Los Angeles on Saturday at American Family Field, and manager Dave Roberts said Rojas likely would be part of the NLCS roster.

Rojas, 37, hit a tying homer in the ninth inning of Game 7 of the World Series last year at Toronto, helping the Dodgers win their second straight championship. He has said he is leaning toward retiring at the end of the season.

The addition of Wrobleski gives the Dodgers 13 pitchers on their NLCS roster after they went with 12 against the Braves. The 26-year-old Wrobleski went 12-5 with a 3.66 ERA in 22 starts and six relief appearances this year, making the NL All-Star team for the first time.

Infielder Hyeseong Kim was left off the Dodgers' NLCS roster. He appeared in one game against Atlanta as a defensive replacement.

stories.headline: George Russell praises Red Bull after upgrade success and consecutive wins: 'Team to beat'
stories.summary: George Russell has said Red Bull is now "the team to beat" in Formula 1 after Max Verstappen secured his second grand prix victory in a row at Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
George Russell has said Red Bull is now "the team to beat" in Formula 1 after Max Verstappen secured his second grand prix victory in a row at Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen's win in Singapore followed a sprint victory on the same circuit on Saturday and his first grand prix victory of 2026 last weekend at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Mercedes' strong start to the season means Russell's teammate Kimi Antonelli looks destined to win the drivers' title this season while the German manufacturer has a comfortable margin in the constructors' standings.

But Russell, who finished ninth in Singapore after starting 19th with an engine penalty, believes Verstappen's performance at the last three rounds means Red Bull has surpassed Mercedes as the best team on the grid.

"I think the main thing for us as a team is to try and understand how we're going to find more performance because the performance of Red Bull has been very impressive the last three weeks on three very different circuits and you know right now they are the team to beat," Russell said.

"The goal right now is we need to understand how to get more out of this [upgrade] package. Kimi ran it, the numbers say it's performing as we expect but obviously the lap times haven't been that great so we need to try and understand how to make that work."

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff also praised Red Bull's improvement in the second half of the year and believes they will be a title challenger in 2027.

- Lewis Hamilton calls Singapore GP strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

"Really, you need to take your hat off of what Red Bull has done this season, how they have developed the car and how it's all come together as a package," Wolff said.

"And then you put Max Verstappen in the car and when he feels that this thing is driving like he wants it to drive, then these are the results. He's been by far the quickest guy today. He's been the quickest guy in Kuala Lumpur.

"Let's see when our upgrade hopefully starts to work and land in a place where we think it should be, whether we can be competitive against him. But one thing is for sure, next year it's a full-on fight between the teams and Red Bull is part of that."

stories.headline: Denkey's double sparks Cincinnati to win over Atlanta
stories.summary: Kevin Denkey scored two goals after a scoreless first half and FC Cincinnati snapped a six-match winless streak with a 3-1 victory over Atlanta United on Saturday night.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- Kevin Denkey scored two goals after a scoreless first half and FC Cincinnati snapped a six-match winless streak with a 3-1 victory over Atlanta United on Saturday night.

Denkey scored in the 52nd minute to give Cincinnati (9-9-9) a 1-0 lead. Tom Barlow and David Douděra had assists.

Miguel Almirón used passes from Breel Embolo and Tomás Jacob to score his fifth goal and tie it 1-all in the 69th minute.

Kyle Smith set up Tom Barlow for the go-ahead goal in the 84th minute, and Denkey scored in the seventh minute of stoppage time to wrap up the victory.

Denkey has 16 goals on the season, one more than he had last year in his first 29 league appearances.

Barlow has eight goals and four assists this season - both career highs through 200 career matches.

Evan Louro turned away five shots in his third start in goal this season for Cincinnati and the eighth of his career.

Lucas Hoyos had one save for Atlanta United (7-15-6) in his first MLS campaign.

Cincinnati improves to 2-7-6 on the road while ending an 0-3-3 stretch overall. The club beat Atlanta United 2-0 at home in the season opener to complete the sweep.

Atlanta United saw a three-match unbeaten run end while falling to 4-8-2 at home.

Up next Cincinnati: Hosts New England Revolution on Wednesday.

Atlanta: At CF Montreal on Wednesday.

stories.headline: Inside the abrupt ending to A'ja Wilson's historic MVP season
stories.summary: The WNBA Finals will be without five-time MVP A'ja Wilson and the Aces. The script flipped suddenly on the defending champs.
stories.body:
WITH THE HOOD on her black Aces sweatshirt pulled up, A'ja Wilson walked to the dais 40 minutes after the buzzer sounded on the Aces' season. Her black smiley-face slippers clopped against the stairs. She sat down and drummed her fingers on the table as she fielded questions about why the Aces came up short and what the team's future holds.

She looked down at her lap when Chelsea Gray praised her season.

"MVP, man, that girl can ball. She can hoop," Gray said, earning a sadness-tinged smile and chuckle from Wilson.

It wasn't the ending Wilson envisioned. She shot just 6-for-19 from the floor on Friday night in Las Vegas, missed three free throws in the fourth quarter, and got her pocket picked with 1:54 to go. The turnover allowed the Valkyries to tie the score with a bucket on the other end.

The defending champions never led again.

On the next possession, Wilson missed a jumper in the lane and the Valkyries scored again to go up by two. A Jackie Young bucket forced overtime, but the Aces were outscored 16-6 and were swept out of the WNBA semifinals with an 87-77 loss.

"I want to do everything I can for my team, and I felt like I did not do that at some points," Wilson said at the dais. "So I think that is going to carry over more so than [missing] the free throw or the missed shots."

Wilson's record-breaking fifth MVP season concluded far sooner than she imagined, on a night when she scored 21 points and grabbed 10 rebounds. All season long, she showcased her evolving game. She's a better shooter, a better facilitator, a better defender. But even her greatness has limits. Injuries to teammates, a suffocating Valkyries defense and a pointing fan in Indiana proved too much for even the greatest to overcome.

A DAY BEFORE the official demise, Wilson wore a double-breasted Aces red Dolce & Gabbana suit and was flanked by her five MVP trophies. She peered through her black-rimmed glasses as she addressed reporters after receiving her record fifth WNBA MVP trophy and unprecedented third in a row.

"It truly means a lot, and so I think that's why I cried a little bit harder on this one," Wilson said Thursday. "Because 15-year-old A'ja wasn't sitting up here dreaming about being a five-time MVP. She wasn't dreaming about being a three-time champion. She was dreaming about surviving this world. For me to sit up here surrounded by these trophies and to be able to play the game of basketball every single day just means a little bit more to me."

Surprised by her teammates and WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert at practice, Wilson doubled over in tears. Her mother, Eva Rakes Wilson, carried in the newest award for her daughter's stuffed trophy case. Engelbert presented a cream-colored old-fashioned phone to Wilson preloaded with congratulatory messages. She heard from her family, former coaches, each of her teammates, her partner Bam Adebayo, and Kamala Harris, the former vice president and Wilson's fellow Alpha Kappa Alpha alum.

"Keep being the example. Keep being you," Dawn Staley told Wilson in her message.

"Little girls around the world, they see you," Lisa Leslie said.

"You are the blueprint of what an elite athlete should strive to be," Sylvia Fowles told her.

"This game needed you. Vegas needed you. We all needed you," Chelsea Gray said.

"Quite frankly, the planet hasn't seen anything like you," Becky Hammon said.

Wilson had come a long way from the young girl in Columbia, South Carolina, who spent her time handing out water bottles to her teammates because she wasn't good enough to get on the floor.

Now she's arguably the best women's basketball player in history.

Wilson dominated the MVP conversation practically from the jump. She dropped 45 points against Connecticut on May 15 and swept the WNBA's Western Conference Player of the Month awards all season.

Other players had their moments of MVP contention -- Olivia Miles, Paige Bueckers, Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell -- but their theoretical viability faded as Wilson's inevitability emerged. Again.

"They want to pick someone else, but she won't let them," Adebayo said in an August phone interview. "If you look at the numbers, there's no way you can't. Like how do you give it to someone else?"

Wilson finished the regular season as the league's scoring champion, averaging 26.2 points per game and topping 1,000 points for the second time in her career. She has expanded her playmaking ability and averaged a career-high 3.2 assists per game. Wilson also stepped out on the perimeter and shot a career-best 40.4% from beyond the arc. Her 9.4 win shares led the league, 1.9 higher than second place. Her 32.4 efficiency rating (PER) was similarly dominant with the league's second-highest at 24.1. Wilson has posted four of the WNBA's top seven single-season efficiency ratings from 2023-26, and is the career PER leader.

When Wilson was awarded her first MVP in 2020, the Aces were swept in the WNBA Finals by Seattle. The young superstar was among the best in the league. It was Hammon's arrival that helped make her the best.

HAMMON WATCHED AS WILSON drilled shots from around the perimeter, far beyond what Hammon thought her natural range was. Hammon had just taken the job as the Aces' head coach, and Wilson had flown to San Antonio to meet with her. They'd gone out to dinner at a Brazilian steakhouse the night before so Hammon could get to know her new star. She had a request.

"I asked her to allow me to coach her," Hammon recalled in August. "And coach her hard in front of her teammates, which she agreed to. She's a real one."

The next day, Hammon put Wilson through a workout to get a close look at the talent she wanted to push. She'd seen Wilson's low-post dominance on film, but this version of Wilson was different. She showed Hammon that she was capable of more than she'd put on tape to that point. When Hammon asked why Wilson wasn't more active on the perimeter, Wilson said it wasn't part of the previous system.

"I was like, 'Well, it's about to be part of the system,'" Hammon said.

Wilson consistently showed off that evolution this season. Against the Valkyries on June 21, Golden State guard Tiffany Hayes drove down the lane. Wilson turned her body toward Hayes and bent her knees to prepare to explode upward. As Hayes floated the ball toward the rim, Wilson leapt with her left arm fully outstretched, twisting her body to avoid Hayes as she drove by and swatted the ball.

Jewell Loyd grabbed the deflection and passed the ball back to Wilson, who threw it ahead to Young before sprinting up the court. Young flicked the ball back to a trailing Wilson. The 6-foot-4 center caught the pass in stride, dribbled by her defender and finished the layup with her left hand.

Just another highlight for the five-time MVP and three-time Defensive Player of the Year.

"She's just extended her game," Hammon said in July. "She's not just a low-block elbow type of player, which she very much was when I first got here. Now, we play her like a big guard a lot of times, and she's just a nightmare matchup for people. I don't know if anybody's found the remedy for her."

Wilson put in the work during her offseason. Unlike many WNBA stars, Wilson doesn't play competitively in the months between WNBA seasons. Fans and competitors alike won't see her in Unrivaled or dominating overseas in the EuroLeague. After the WNBA season ends, she takes a few months off to recharge. And then, when she hears the call of the ball bouncing on the hardwood, Wilson goes to work.

"When it comes to basketball, the way that I view it, like it's just a matter of sharpening tools," Wilson said in July. "You have those tools already in your toolbox. It's just a matter of how you use them and if you can sharpen them."

Wilson has focused during the past three offseasons on navigating the tight windows presented to her on the court. The pirouettes through double-teams, slipping through traffic on drives to the basket, a jab step to create space, a reverse pivot to a face-up jumper, her ability to maneuver within and manipulate cramped spaces elevated her game.

"You'll see her at the elbow now, between the legs, into a combo move," Gray said in August. "You think you got her figured out and the next year she comes with something better."

"I don't want to call her a maniac, but [she's got] the mindset of somebody that is obsessed to be that great and just dominant from all levels," Adebayo said.

THE FIRST REAL SIGN of trouble for Wilson emerged on Aug. 31 when USA Basketball announced she wouldn't play in the FIBA Women's World Cup because of a nagging back injury. She'd missed four games in late June and early July, including the Commissioner's Cup championship against New York, due to an ankle injury, but she'd played at a high level through July and August. Not going to Berlin was the first indication that something was amiss with her body.

The break, however, was good physically and mentally for Wilson. She practiced with her teammates while Young and Gray won a gold medal overseas. As she worked to get healthy, Wilson moved lighter in the gym and the locker room, giving her teammates more glimpses of her humor and goofiness.

"She was just more opened up," Aces forward Cheyenne Parker-Tyus said at shootaround before Game 2 against the Fever. "Throughout the season, she's reserved, you know, because it takes a lot. I think that has to do with just everybody always constantly pulling at her, and the world is literally on her shoulders sometimes. But she was definitely more giddy and more just in a good place. You could tell that she was happy to be home. Sometimes, when you're dealing with injuries and pains, it can affect your mental."

Off the court, Wilson relaxed with her dogs, watched movies with her parents, swam and enjoyed massages. "She got a lot of self-care and relaxation," Rakes Wilson said. "And it shows. She was ready to go."

In the four games following the FIBA break that closed the regular season, Wilson looked rejuvenated, averaging 27.8 points, 8.8 rebounds, 3.8 assists, 1.3 steals and 1.3 blocks during the stretch. And in Game 1 against the Fever, Wilson was transcendent: 38 points, 16 rebounds, 4 blocks and 2 steals.

"She's ready to go," Hammon said of Wilson after the Aces' Game 1 102-85 victory. "She understands the stakes always. She was a clinic tonight. There was nothing she didn't do tonight."

Wilson often says, "The crown is heavy." Sometimes it wobbles.

CHAOS ERUPTED SUDDENLY in Game 2 on Sept. 29 in Indiana. Wilson and Fever guard Sophie Cunningham collided in the lane with 4:10 to go in the fourth quarter. Cunningham ended up on the hardwood, and Wilson stumbled forward to regain her balance. Referees called a blocking foul on Cunningham.

An expressionless Wilson walked off the collision. As she approached the basket, she locked eyes with a Fever fan standing and pointing at her. According to another fan in the section, the pointing fan shouted, "That's on you!" referring to the foul just called on Cunningham.

Wilson accelerated toward the fan, crossed the white painted boundary of the baseline and bent toward him. She yelled, "You don't point at me!" Her teammates and coaches rushed to pull her away. Wilson was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike conduct.

After the game, Wilson said she apologized to her teammates for the technical but defended her actions. "I try to play my game ... but if I am just walking, just got the foul, I'm chilling and I see a man come at me, taking steps toward me and pointing at me, I don't give a damn what you said," she said. "I don't give a damn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable. You don't step toward me. You never should sit and point at me. That there is unacceptable."

For the entirety of Wilson's athletic career, she's been known for her charisma, humility and gratitude. The outburst in Gainbridge was discombobulating largely because Wilson isn't known for fiery displays. She celebrates -- who doesn't love a good A'ja stomp after an and-1? -- makes faces and complains to refs as much as the next player. What happened in Indianapolis was something different.

It was an out-of-character moment toward the end of an out-of-character performance for Wilson. In the Aces' 99-89 Game 2 loss, she had 22 points and nine rebounds, but it was far from the dominance she displayed in Game 1. And the moment between her and the fan she confronted became the first significant controversy of her career.

She was criticized by some on social media for overreacting. Cunningham, who declined an interview request through her agent for this story, told Wilson to "grow up" on her podcast.

"I could care less about what anyone has to say about me or anything they want to write about me or comment," Wilson said. "No one's ever lived this life that I'm living, so they can never have any input that would make my mind go into another space. I really don't care about it."

Others -- teammates and family -- empathized with her reaction during an intense game in a hostile road arena.

"That's not A'ja," Rakes Wilson said. "She's managed in the whole nine years of her career not to do what she did, so it had to be something. And I'll be honest with you, I don't care what he said. That's not important to me. What's important to me was she felt unsafe, she felt threatened, and she felt disrespected."

Wilson received no additional punishment for her actions, and neither did the Aces players who left the bench to pull her back. The Aces won Game 3 at home and the world kept spinning. But the Aces and Wilson didn't win again.

IN GAME 1 against the Valkyries, the Aces managed just 60 points, their lowest total of the season. Jewell Loyd hurt her leg in the third quarter and didn't return. Game 2 was closer even without Loyd, but a furious rally came up short. And suddenly the reigning champions were facing elimination in Game 3.

Wilson arrived at her home arena on Friday in a white T-shirt and shorts. She sidestepped the pomp and circumstance that has come to characterize WNBA arrivals. No glitzy outfit. No pregame autographs. No trophies. Her parents lifted Wilson's MVP trophy for the crowd in a pregame ceremony, while Wilson warmed up with her teammates.

"The individual award is going to be what it's going to be," Wilson said. "I love it. I cherish it. I don't take it for granted. But the main goal is always going to be a championship."

For a half, the Aces looked like they could keep their goal intact. But they were outscored 17-7 in the third quarter and then lost a late lead in the fourth. Shots clanged off the rim. Turnovers mounted. The Aces were done.

With her parents and Adebayo waiting, Wilson sat at the podium and insisted they were done only for now.

"It's just not our time, and I'm OK with that," she said. "I'm at peace with the great things we did do. I can't harp on this game too much. I'm just very happy that our team was locked in and we showed up for one another. Obviously the outcome's not what we wanted, but we're still champions at heart. We're gonna have another opportunity. I guarantee you that."

stories.headline: Saints AFLW coach steps down as club plans review
stories.summary: Embattled St Kilda AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo has stepped down amid the club's winless season.
stories.body:
Embattled St Kilda AFLW coach Nick Dal Santo has stepped down amid the club's winless season.

The last-placed Saints will conduct a review into their AFLW program, led by former Carlton football boss Brad Lloyd, in the wake of Dal Santo's departure.

Dal Santo, a St Kilda great as a player, was in his sixth season at the Saints and will coach his final game against Collingwood on Saturday, before departing.

"I've been giving a lot of thought to my future and whether continuing in this role was the right decision, both for myself and the program," Dal Santo said in a statement.

"Where we've been able to take this program is something I'll always be incredibly proud of.

"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.

"I have a strong love for this club, I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.

"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."

The Saints will have three games left in the season after Saturday, when they will attempt to amend their unwanted record of being the only winless team in the competition.

"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda chief executive Carl Dilena said in a statement

"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden final's appearance last season.

"We look forward to recognising Nick's contribution this weekend as he leads the team one final time in front of our members and supporters at RSEA Park."

Lloyd will lead the review, via Apogee Sports, during the remainder of the season, while the Saints start their hunt for their next coach.

"Our ambition is to be a consistently competitive and respected club that can contend with the best in the competition," Dilena said.

"We want to give our AFLW program every chance to achieve this and that means identifying where we need to improve, investing in the right areas and acting with urgency."

stories.headline: New Zealand Rugby launches legal action against ARLC over 'Chiefs' name
stories.summary: The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.
stories.body:
The battle over the use of the "Chiefs" name is headed to the New Zealand High Court after New Zealand Rugby launched legal action against the Australian Rugby League Commission.

NZR on Thursday said it had been left with no choice but to launch legal proceedings against the ARLC, who has sought to adopt the name for its Papua New Guinea expansion franchise.

The PNG Chiefs are due to join the NRL in 2028 and have already signed a raft of players, including code-hoppers Zac Lomaz and Joey Manu, but they may yet have to undergo a chanGe of name if NZR gets its way.

The Chiefs' Super Rugby franchise has existed since 1996, with NZR claiming the introduction of the PNG Chiefs would result in "significant confusion and damage" should they be allowed to compete under the name from 2028.

"New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has today moved to protect the Chiefs brand and is filing proceedings in the High Court of New Zealand against the decision by the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) to launch a new NRL side using "Chiefs" in its name," an NZR statement read.  

"NZR is seeking both an interim and final injunction which stops the use of the names 'PNG Chiefs', 'Chiefs' or any other similar names in New Zealand.   

"The Chiefs have competed as a professional rugby team in Super Rugby since 1996 and over those 30 years, have built a strong identity and fanbase across New Zealand, Australia and internationally.  

"In New Zealand, NZR owns both the trademark rights for the word Chiefs and the Chiefs logo and since 1998, NZR has also held trademark protection for the Chiefs logo in Australia."

NZR claims it had tried to engage with the ARLC in an attempt to find a resolution, yet the commission was now intent on proceeding with the official launch of the PNG Chiefs on Oct. 21.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said. "We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand.   

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific. We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."  

The Chiefs won two Super Rugby titles in back-to-back seasons in 2012 and 2013, and were runners-up in Super Rugby Pacific this season after suffering a crushing defeat by the Hurricanes in the decider.

The Hamilton-based team has produced countless All Blacks since its inception, with Saturday's run-on team to face the Wallabies featuring six players from the franchise.

"Here in New Zealand, when people hear 'the Chiefs', they think of this club and this region. The identity carries significant cultural meaning and connection to the region and its people, we know it means a great deal to our players and coaches past and present, fans and supporters here and around the world," Chiefs CEO Simon Graafhuis said.   

"Teams in different sports and markets can exist alongside one another with the same name, but the issue here is the similarity of our sports competing in the same market, for the same fans, in overlapping windows."  

However, ARLC executive chairman Peter V'Landys later issued a stinging rebuke, insisting he would vigorously defend PNG's right to use the Chiefs as its team name.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval. The NSW Blues had been the Blues for in excess of 50 years before that," he said.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

No date has yet been slated for the hearing in New Zealand's High Court.
